paragraphs.source_en: Meitei said, “Well, well! Are you trying to use this critical moment to avenge yourself for that peacock’s tongue of mine?” “I am not a braggart like you.” The master said this calmly, twisting his moustache. Mr. Meitei spoke as though he were the very head of aesthetic judgment: “They say that long ago someone asked Rai Sanyo, ‘Sir, have you seen any fine writing lately?’ Sanyo showed him a dunning letter written by a packhorse driver and said, ‘This may be called the finest writing of recent days.’ It may be that your aesthetic eye is surprisingly sound. Well then, read it aloud, and I shall criticize it.”

paragraphs.source_en: Kate looked out through the window, and a group of children were playing at throwing a ball. They threw the ball high up into the air. The ball went higher and higher. After a while, the ball came down. They threw it high again, and again and again; every time they threw it, it came down. Kate asked, “Why does it come down? Why does it not keep flying upward?” Her mother answered, “Because a giant lives underground. He is Giant Gravitation. He is strong, and he pulls all things toward himself. He pulls houses down to the ground; if he did not pull them, the houses would fly away. Children would fly away too. You have seen leaves fall; that too is Giant Gravitation calling them. Sometimes you drop a book to the floor; that too is because Giant Gravitation says, ‘Come here.’ When the ball is thrown into the air, Giant Gravitation calls it, and so it comes down.”

paragraphs.source_en: Meitei said, “Is that all?” The master said, “Mm. Isn’t it beautifully written?” Meitei said, “Well, I must say I am beaten. I never expected you to return my Tochimenbo here.” The master said, “It is not a return blow at all. The piece is genuinely good, so I translated it. Do you not think so?” The master searched the expression hidden behind Meitei’s gold-rimmed spectacles. “I am astonished that you possess such skill. Yes, this time I have truly been made a fool of. I surrender! I surrender!” Meitei set his glib tongue in motion and laughed it off on his own. The master did not understand his meaning in the least and said, “I had no intention of making you surrender. I only translated it because I thought it was an extremely interesting piece.” “No, it is truly interesting. If you had not done it this way, it would not be the real thing. Terrific. I am completely humbled.” “There is no need for you to be humbled. Since I have lately stopped painting watercolors, I thought I might try my hand at writing instead.” “How could this talent be compared with your watercolors, where near and far are indistinguishable and black and white are equal? I am admiration itself!” The master said, “When you praise me like that, I feel still more inclined to go on.” It seems the master’s understanding and what Meitei was saying were at cross purposes to the very end.
